title: Supplier Hotfix Rollback and Hotpatch Escrow Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook provides a contract-adjacent exhibit and operational checklist for: (a) contractual escrow of hotfix artifacts and validated hotpatch procedures from third-party inference suppliers; and (b) standardized rollback mechanics for customer-managed or Redwood-operated private deployments. The goal is to reduce MTTD/MTTR for customer-facing degradation while preserving auditability and minimal data exposure.

Scope:
Applies to third-party suppliers and partners who provide model binaries, serving runtime patches, or configuration changes that may be applied to Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) deployments or Dedicated pools. Not intended for purely hosted API integrations where Redwood controls deployment pipeline (exception: when supplier-provided code is installed into customer-dedicated runtimes).

Key Definitions (contract-friendly language):
- Hotfix: a change intended to remediate a production-impacting defect in the inference stack or model weights that must be applied outside of a regular release cadence.
- Hotpatch: a binary or configuration change that can be applied in-place with no data migration but may alter runtime behavior (e.g., kernel switch, new quantization shim).
- Escrow Package: a time-stamped, signed bundle stored with a mutually agreed escrow agent or customer-controlled storage containing artifacts required to revert or apply hotfixes.
- Rollback Window: the period after a hotfix during which supplier and customer coordinate an automatic or manual revert if SLOs or safety checks fail.

Triggering Events (examples):
- Critical latency regression > 30% above baseline for > 5 minutes measured at the model route level.
- Safety filter bypass causing customer-visible PII leakage or policy violation.
- Deterministic output change correlated to a model binary update that increases error rate beyond contract acceptance thresholds.

Escrow Package Minimum Contents:
- Signed manifest (JSON) with artifact hashes, semantic version, and compatibility constraints (hardware, runtime ABI, quantization profile).
- Executable patch artifacts and reverse patch (revert script) where possible, with checksums.
- Repro scripts to validate presence/absence of fix in a customer-like environment (small fixture dataset).
- Minimal README including expected SLO impact, preconditions, and rollback steps.
- Cryptographic signing material and supplier contact escalation tree.
- Redaction notes indicating any customer- or Redwood-owned secrets that must not be escrowed.

Operational Flow (summary):
1. Pre-authorize: Contract exhibit requires supplier to deliver Escrow Package to escrow repository at least on hotfix submission. Pre-production validation checklist agreed in contract.
2. Pre-announce: Supplier notifies Redwood and affected customers with a short description, risk matrix, and proposed maintenance window.
3. Staging validation: Suppliers provide automated validation scripts run by Redwood in a staging environment that mirrors production config.
4. Go/No-go gating: Rollout allowed only if staging passes baseline checks and security scan of artifacts.
5. Deployment: Hotpatch applied with a short canary cohort and telemetry instrumentation ramp.
6. Monitoring & rollback: If rollback triggers fire, automatic safe revert executed per rubric and post-mortem initiated.

Rollback Mechanics (detailed):
- Automatic rollback triggers (examples): sustained error rate > 2x baseline for 10 minutes; safety violation signatures; KV-cache mismatch errors causing inference failures.
- Manual rollback: authorized Redwood on-call + supplier engineer authorization required for manual revert outside automatic triggers.
- Revert execution: pull escrowed revert artifact by hash, validate signature, apply in controlled sequence (canary -> rest-of-fleet).
- Data considerations: for any patch that mutates persisted model formats, the revert must include migration scripts or fallback stored copies. Revert must not depend on deleted user data.

Auditability & Evidence Collection:
- All hotfix actions logged to the deployment audit trail with: operator identity, artifact hash, start/end timestamps, telemetry snapshot (latency, error rate), and link to escrow package.
- Suppliers must provide signed attestations for each escrowed artifact release.
- For on-prem deployments, a lightweight evidence manifest must be appended to customer audit storage (hashes + signed attestation) and made available for periodic review.

SLA, Credits, and Financial Remedies:
- Time-to-first-fix commitment: Supplier acknowledges first triage response within contracted hours (e.g., 4 hrs business).
- Rollback service level: If a rollbackable hotfix causes customer downtime and supplier does not honor rollback playbook within defined window, supplier pays specified service credits proportional to affected route revenue. Exact credit calc to be negotiated per-customer.

Security & Secret Handling:
- Escrow packages must not contain customer private keys or KMS materials. Any necessary secrets must be obtained from customer at application-time via secure injection, not stored in escrow.
- Supplier-signed artifacts must be scanned by Redwood SCA tools; binary analysis and SBOM extraction required before allowlist decision.

Customer Communication Templates (snippet):
Subject: Planned Hotfix for [model/route] — Proposed Window [date/time]
Body: Short summary of issue, expected impact, staging results link, canary plan, rollback criteria and contact list. Attach: public portion of escrow manifest.

Contract Exhibit Language (suggested clauses, high-level):
- Escrow Delivery Obligation: Supplier shall deposit an Escrow Package with [escrow agent/customer-specified storage] within 24 hours of hotfix approval.
- Revertability Warranty: Supplier warrants that every hotfix will be accompanied by a revert artifact that allows restoration to the pre-hotfix state without loss of customer data or loss of required cryptographic verification.
- Audit Right: Customer and Redwood shall have the right to audit escrowed artifacts and request re-provisioning on demand with 48 hours notice.
- Liability Carveouts: Supplier is not liable for pre-existing customer misconfiguration uncovered by hotfix validation steps; supplier remains liable for defects introduced by provided artifacts per main contract terms.

Checklist for Legal/Technical Review Prior to Execution:
- Are artifact hashes present and verified?
- Is there a revert script and communication plan?
- Are SBOM and binary scan results attached?
- Are migration scripts included if model format changes?
- Do escrow artifacts avoid customer secrets?

Open Questions / Items for Negotiation:
- Escrow agent choice (neutral third party vs. customer-managed storage).
- Financial credit formula — flat vs. revenue-proportional.
- Maximum allowed rollback window before enforcement.
- Retention period for escrow packages and access revocation terms.

Appendix A: Example minimal manifest (human-readable):
- name: supplier-model-hotpatch-2026-01
- version: 2026.01.15-hotpatch-3
- compatible_hardware: [A100-80GB, H100]
- artifact_hash: sha256:...
- revert_hash: sha256:...
- sbom_link: ...
- signed_by: engineering-lead@supplier.com

Appendix B: Playbook runbook (short):
- T+0: Supplier pushes escrowed package and notifies Redwood.
- T+1: Redwood runs staging validation within 3 hours.
- T+4: Canary rollout begins if staging passes.
- T+4.5: Full rollout or rollback decision within 30–60 minutes after canary completion.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is written as a contract exhibit + operational SOP hybrid. The intent is to be prescriptive enough for SREs while flexible for legal negotiation.
- Recommend legal weigh in on revertability warranty language and limits on liability.
- Recommend security review of the SBOM/scan gates and a short onboarding checklist for suppliers who will be placed on the hotfix rotation.

Change log:
- 2025-11-03 A. Patel initial draft.
- 2026-01-12 L. Ortiz added rollback triggers and manifest example.
- 2026-02-20 M. Green added SLA/credit placeholders and playbook runbook.
